blocks.content: RAID, Redundant Array of Independent Disks, is the technique of combining several physical drives into one logical unit to improve reliability, performance, or some real, honest tradeoff between the two. This chapter closes out the File Systems and Storage module by moving from a single physical drive, the subject of the previous chapter, to arrays of them.

This is squarely a reliability and performance topic, not a backup replacement, and that distinction gets stated plainly and repeated throughout this chapter, echoing the same honest line the journaling chapter drew for a completely different mechanism.
1. Why RAID Exists

A single physical disk, whether an HDD or an SSD, both covered in the previous chapter, is a single point of failure. If it dies, every file stored on it is gone, in full, with no partial recovery possible from the drive itself. It is also a single performance bottleneck, since only one drive worth of read and write throughput is ever available no matter how much data needs moving.

RAID addresses both of these limitations by combining multiple physical drives into one logical unit that the rest of the system treats as if it were a single drive. Different RAID levels make genuinely different choices about how those multiple drives are used, and the rest of this chapter works through the most important ones in order.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197680-336413425.png

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: RAID combines multiple physical drives into one logical unit specifically to improve reliability, performance, or a deliberate tradeoff between the two, not to serve as a backup.
2. RAID 0: Striping

RAID 0 splits data into chunks and spreads them, striped, evenly across every drive in the array. Because different chunks of the same file live on different physical drives, multiple drives can be read from or written to simultaneously, genuinely boosting throughput compared to any single drive alone.

The cost has to be stated with complete honesty: RAID 0 provides zero redundancy. Since each individual drive holds only a fragment of every file rather than a full independent copy of anything, losing even one single drive in the array destroys access to essentially every file, not just the fraction that happened to live on that specific drive.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197681-995905077.png
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197681-276837341.png
3. RAID 1: Mirroring

RAID 1 takes the opposite approach. Every single piece of data is duplicated, written identically, to two or more drives at once. If one drive fails completely, the mirror drive still holds a full, complete, independent copy of everything, and the system keeps running with no data lost at all.

The cost here is capacity, stated plainly: effective usable storage is cut in half, or worse with more mirrors, for a given amount of raw physical disk purchased. Two 1TB drives mirrored together provide 1TB of usable, reliable storage, not 2TB.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197681-52580799.png
4. RAID 5: Striping With Parity

RAID 5 is a popular middle ground between RAID 0 and RAID 1. Data is striped across drives, exactly like RAID 0, for a real performance benefit, but an additional parity block, extra recovery information mathematically computed from the other data blocks, is also distributed across the drives alongside the actual data.

If any single drive in the array fails, the data it held can be fully mathematically reconstructed using the parity information together with the data on the surviving drives. RAID 5 requires a minimum of three drives to work at all, and it honestly can only survive exactly one simultaneous drive failure, not two, if a second drive fails before the first is replaced and rebuilt, the array loses data.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197681-774581379.png
5. RAID 10: Combining Mirroring and Striping

RAID 10, sometimes written 1+0, combines both previous ideas directly. Drives are first mirrored in pairs for reliability, exactly like RAID 1, and then data is striped across those already mirrored pairs for performance, exactly like RAID 0.

This genuinely gets strong benefits of both approaches at once, solid read and write performance from striping, and solid fault tolerance from mirroring. The real honest cost is needing a larger minimum number of physical drives to set up at all, and, like RAID 1, roughly halving usable capacity compared to the raw total purchased.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197682-565166039.png
6. Comparing RAID 0, 1, 5, and 10

7. A Worked Example: Four 1TB Drives
Concrete numbers make the tradeoffs unmistakable. Take four physical drives, each 1TB, and compare the actual usable capacity and fault tolerance under each RAID level.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197682-461047784.png

{"headers":["RAID level","Usable capacity with 4x1TB","Simultaneous drive failures survived"],"rows":[["RAID 0","4TB, all four drives striped with no redundancy","0, any single failure loses the array"],["RAID 1","2TB if mirrored as two pairs, or 1TB if all four mirror one dataset","Up to half the drives, as long as at least one full copy survives"],["RAID 5","3TB, one drive worth of capacity spent on distributed parity","1, exactly"],["RAID 10","2TB, two mirrored pairs striped together","1 guaranteed, up to 2 if the two failures land in different mirrored pairs"]]}

Notice RAID 5 delivers the most usable capacity of the three redundant options here, 3TB out of 4TB raw, while RAID 10 trades capacity for generally faster rebuild and better performance under heavy simultaneous read and write load.
8. RAID Is Not a Backup

This distinction deserves to be stated as plainly as possible, echoing the exact same honest line the journaling chapter drew between crash consistency and real backups. RAID protects against a physical drive failure specifically. It does not protect against accidental deletion, a file corrupted at the software or file system level, ransomware encrypting every file it can reach, or an entire building or site level disaster.

If a user deletes the wrong file, RAID will faithfully and correctly propagate that deletion across every drive in the array, because from RAID own point of view that was a perfectly valid, successfully completed write. Real world reliability requires both RAID, for hardware fault tolerance, and actual, ideally offsite, backups, for every other failure mode RAID was never designed to handle.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197682-528780148.png

blocks.title: A distinction worth repeating
blocks.content: RAID is a hardware fault tolerance mechanism, not a backup strategy. Treating a RAID array as if it were a backup is one of the most common and costly misunderstandings in storage system design, and it tends to surface at the worst possible moment, right after data has already been lost to something RAID was never built to prevent.
9. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Believing RAID, of any level, is an adequate substitute for real backups, when it only ever protects against a physical drive failure and nothing else.","Mistaking RAID 5 parity reconstruction for surviving any number of simultaneous drive failures, when it specifically and only survives exactly one.","Assuming RAID 0 offers any redundancy at all simply because multiple drives are involved, when it offers none, and is strictly a performance technique."]
items: Believing RAID, of any level, is an adequate substitute for real backups, when it only ever protects against a physical drive failure and nothing else.
Mistaking RAID 5 parity reconstruction for surviving any number of simultaneous drive failures, when it specifically and only survives exactly one.
Assuming RAID 0 offers any redundancy at all simply because multiple drives are involved, when it offers none, and is strictly a performance technique.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to compute usable capacity and state fault tolerance for RAID 0, 1, 5, and 10 given a specific number and size of drives, exactly like the worked four drive example in this chapter, and be ready to state clearly why RAID is not a backup.

This closes the File Systems and Storage module. From the file abstraction itself, through directories, inodes, allocation methods, journaling for crash consistency, disk scheduling and the physical SSD and HDD hardware layer, all the way up to RAID combining multiple physical drives, this module has traced the complete real path data takes from a user saving a file down to the physical medium it ultimately rests on.
